lookup_file: config/fhir_map.yaml says how to find each test, fact and chart observation in FHIR. This file names them by id only.
review_status: DRAFT - written using guidelines listed in 'sources', from memory (the guideline sites blocked automated reading). Items marked 'verify' must be checked against the guideline text. Every flag, test, option and threshold needs cardiologist review before use.

sources.aha_chest_pain_2021: 2021 AHA/ACC/ASE/CHEST/SAEM/SCCT/SCMR Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain
sources.acc_afib_2023: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation
sources.nice_ng106: NICE NG106 Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management (2018)
sources.nice_qs9: NICE QS9 Chronic heart failure in adults (quality standard)
sources.aha_hf_2022: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
sources.aha_bp_2017_2025: ACC/AHA Guideline for High Blood Pressure in Adults (2017; updated 2025)
sources.acc_brady_2018: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay
sources.aha_chol_2018: 2018 AHA/ACC Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol (NOT in Rhea's source list - added for the cholesterol half of reason 5)
sources.aha_qt_2010: 2010 AHA/ACCF Scientific Statement on Prevention of Torsade de Pointes in Hospital Settings (NOT in Rhea's source list - added for long QT)

tiers.emergent: Needs the ER now - not a referral. Card says 'advise ER now'.
tiers.urgent: Specialist within about 2 weeks (matches NICE's 2-week heart failure rule).
tiers.routine: Normal queue. Some routine cases have a 'soon' hint (e.g. NICE 6-week heart failure rule) shown on the card but not a separate tier.

family_history.text: Family history of early heart disease (from the referral note)

prior_mi_cad.text: Prior heart attack, coronary disease, stent or bypass

prior_stroke_tia.text: Prior stroke, TIA or blood clot

vascular_disease.text: Vascular disease (prior heart attack, peripheral artery disease)

av_nodal_meds.text: Medicines that slow the heart or conduction

amlodipine.text: On amlodipine or nifedipine (can cause ankle swelling)

hf_worsening_meds.text: Medicines that can worsen heart failure

np_lowering_meds.text: Heart medicines that can lower NT-proBNP

prior_cardiac_testing.text: Earlier stress test or coronary angiogram

accompanying_symptoms.text: Accompanying symptoms (nausea, fatigue, breathlessness, jaw/arm/back pain)

ecg_compare_prior.name: Compare with a prior ECG
ecg_compare_prior.note: 'done' means an earlier ECG exists to compare against

out_of_office_bp.name: Home or ambulatory BP monitoring to confirm readings

stress_or_ccta.name: Stress test or coronary CT (type chosen by cardiology)

er_precautions.text: Give clear 'call 911 / go to the ER if...' instructions

review_bp_lipid_meds.text: Review blood pressure and cholesterol medicines

risk_factor_modification.text: Address weight, alcohol, sleep apnea and activity (AFib risk factors)

anticoag_decision.text: Blood-thinner (stroke prevention) decision - for the specialist

rate_control_decision.text: Heart-rate control medicine decision - for the specialist

daily_weights.text: Weigh daily and report fast gain

diuretic_by_specialist.text: Any water-pill (diuretic) change - by the specialist only

review_hf_worsening_meds.text: Review medicines that can worsen heart failure or cause swelling (NSAIDs, pioglitazone, diltiazem/verapamil, amlodipine)

review_qt_meds.text: Review medicines that can prolong the QT interval

review_av_nodal_meds.text: Review medicines that slow the heart (beta blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin, amiodarone)

home_bp_log.text: Keep a home blood pressure log

adherence_check.text: Check whether medicines are being taken as prescribed

review_interfering_meds.text: Review things that raise BP (NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, steroids, oral contraceptives, alcohol)

fits.econsult_enough: eConsult answer is enough - no visit needed

chest_pain.label: Chest pain

red_flags.text: Chest pain at rest or ongoing (possible heart attack - ER by ambulance, don't wait for office tests)
Chest pain with sweating, fainting or breathlessness
Recent chest pain with new ischemic ECG changes
Sudden tearing pain to the back, or sudden breathlessness / coughing blood (aortic dissection or blood clot in lung)

urgent_flags.text: New or worsening chest pain with exertion

decision_facts.group: Known coronary disease: prior heart attack, stent or bypass
decision_facts.why: Known coronary disease changes the testing pathway and raises concern for a new blockage

decision_facts.group: Heart risk factors: age, sex, high BP, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, family history
decision_facts.why: Guideline sorts patients into low / intermediate / high risk to decide whether testing is needed at all

decision_facts.group: Kidney function (eGFR)
decision_facts.why: Coronary CT and some tests use contrast dye, which can harm weak kidneys

decision_facts.group: Most recent cholesterol and A1c
decision_facts.why: Used for risk scoring and to see whether prevention is on track

decision_facts.group: Accompanying symptoms, especially in women: nausea, fatigue, breathlessness, jaw/arm/back pain
decision_facts.why: Guideline drops 'atypical'; women more often have these, and they should not lower concern

decision_facts.group: Previous ECG, stress test, coronary CT or angiogram
decision_facts.why: Recent normal testing may change what is needed; abnormal testing raises concern

not_seen: Pain clearly reproduced by pressing on the chest wall (musculoskeletal)
Reflux-type symptoms with low cardiac risk (GI)
Low-risk patient - guideline says further testing may not be needed (eConsult may be enough)
review_notes: Guideline uses 'cardiac / possible cardiac / noncardiac', not 'typical/atypical' - verify wording
Whether cp_ecg_ischemia should be emergent or urgent when pain is not current

palpitations_afib.label: Palpitations / suspected atrial fibrillation

red_flags.text: Very fast heart rate with low blood pressure or near-fainting (unstable)
Stroke symptoms (face droop, arm weakness, speech trouble)

urgent_flags.text: New AFib with a fast rate
Palpitations with new swelling or breathlessness

decision_facts.group: Stroke-risk factors (CHA2DS2-VASc parts): heart failure, high BP, age 65-74 / 75+, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA/clot, vascular disease (prior heart attack, PAD), female sex
decision_facts.why: Drives the blood-thinner decision. Guideline recommends a blood thinner when yearly stroke risk is about 2%+ (roughly score 2+ in men, 3+ in women) - verify. Lantern shows the parts; the specialist decides.

decision_facts.group: Bleeding-risk factors: prior bleeding, heavy alcohol, NSAID or antiplatelet use, kidney or liver disease, anemia
decision_facts.why: Weighed against stroke risk; modifiable ones should be fixed rather than used as a reason to withhold a blood thinner

decision_facts.group: Already on a blood thinner? (warfarin INR if so)
decision_facts.why: Changes the decision from 'whether' to 'is it working'

decision_facts.group: Thyroid (TSH)
decision_facts.why: Overactive thyroid causes AFib and should be treated first

decision_facts.group: Kidney and liver function
decision_facts.why: Needed to choose and dose blood thinners

decision_facts.group: AFib drivers: obesity, sleep apnea, alcohol, high BP
decision_facts.why: 2023 guideline makes risk-factor treatment a core part of AFib care

decision_facts.group: Current heart-rate medicines (beta blocker, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin)
decision_facts.why: Shows whether rate control has been tried

not_seen: Palpitations from an overactive thyroid - may go to endocrinology first
Occasional skipped beats with a normal ECG and no heart disease - often eConsult
review_notes: Exact CHA2DS2-VASc thresholds in the 2023 guideline - verify
Whether Lantern should compute the score or only list the parts

heart_failure_symptoms.label: Heart failure symptoms

red_flags.text: Breathless at rest or can't lie flat

urgent_flags.text: NT-proBNP over 2,000 ng/L (NICE: specialist + echo within 2 weeks)
Fast weight gain or worsening swelling

soon_hints.text: NT-proBNP 400-2,000 ng/L (NICE: specialist + echo within 6 weeks)

decision_facts.group: NT-proBNP value and date
decision_facts.why: NICE uses it to set urgency; below 400 ng/L in an untreated patient makes heart failure less likely - verify

decision_facts.group: Things that push NT-proBNP up: age over 70, AFib, eGFR under 60, lung disease, diabetes
decision_facts.why: A high value may partly reflect these rather than heart failure - verify full NICE list

decision_facts.group: Things that push NT-proBNP down: obesity (BMI over 35), already on diuretic / ACE inhibitor / ARB / beta blocker / MRA
decision_facts.why: A 'normal' value can be falsely reassuring in these patients - verify

decision_facts.group: Prior heart attack, coronary disease, valve disease, high BP, AFib
decision_facts.why: The common causes of heart failure

decision_facts.group: Other causes of swelling: kidney disease, amlodipine, liver disease, low albumin
decision_facts.why: Ankle swelling may not be the heart at all

decision_facts.group: Medicines that can worsen heart failure: NSAIDs, pioglitazone, diltiazem, verapamil
decision_facts.why: Stopping them may help while waiting - specialist decides

decision_facts.group: Hemoglobin, iron studies, thyroid
decision_facts.why: Anemia, iron deficiency and thyroid disease cause or worsen breathlessness; 2022 US guideline recommends iron studies

not_seen: Ankle swelling from a medicine such as amlodipine (PCP med change may be enough)
review_notes: NICE thresholds are for NT-proBNP in ng/L (= pg/mL); BNP uses different cutoffs - verify
Older NICE guidance (CG108) also fast-tracked patients with a prior heart attack; check whether NG106 kept this
Is 2-week = 'urgent' the right mapping for a US clinic?

abnormal_ecg.label: Abnormal ECG

red_flags.text: Signs of an ongoing heart attack
Complete or high-grade heart block with symptoms (fainting, dizziness, breathlessness)
Very slow heart rate with fainting

urgent_flags.text: Mobitz II, 2:1, high-grade or complete heart block - even without symptoms (pacemaker usually indicated)
Long QT (QTc 500 or more is high risk)

decision_facts.group: Earlier ECGs
decision_facts.why: The first question is whether the finding is new or old

decision_facts.group: Prior heart attack or coronary disease
decision_facts.why: Old heart attacks leave lasting ECG changes

decision_facts.group: Medicines that slow the heart or conduction: beta blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin, amiodarone
decision_facts.why: A reversible cause of slow rhythms and blocks

decision_facts.group: QT-prolonging medicines (e.g. citalopram, ondansetron, azithromycin, fluoroquinolones, haloperidol, methadone, sotalol, amiodarone)
decision_facts.why: Common, fixable cause of long QT

decision_facts.group: Potassium, magnesium, calcium, thyroid
decision_facts.why: Low potassium/magnesium/calcium prolong QT; thyroid and potassium affect slow rhythms

decision_facts.group: Sleep apnea
decision_facts.why: Can cause slow heart rates and pauses at night

low_concern_findings: Isolated right bundle branch block without symptoms
not_seen: Unchanged old findings in a patient with no symptoms - often an eConsult answer
Low-concern findings listed in low_concern_findings - usually eConsult
review_notes: Long QT is not covered by the 2018 bradycardia guideline - source and 500 ms cutoff need confirming
How to treat a bundle branch block when no prior ECG exists to show it is new
Echo recommendation for new LBBB - verify in 2018 guideline

hard_to_control_bp_chol.label: Hard-to-control blood pressure or cholesterol

red_flags.text: BP over 180/120 with signs of organ damage: chest pain, confusion, vision change, severe headache, weakness, breathlessness (hypertensive emergency - ER)

urgent_flags.text: BP over 180/120 without signs of organ damage (severe hypertension - not an ER visit; outpatient medicine adjustment)
High BP with low potassium (possible primary aldosteronism)

decision_facts.group: Recent BP readings (trend, not one value)
decision_facts.why: Confirms BP is truly uncontrolled; goal is generally under 130/80 - verify

decision_facts.group: Number and classes of BP medicines, including whether one is a diuretic
decision_facts.why: Resistant hypertension = above goal on 3 medicines (one a diuretic) at good doses, or needing 4+

decision_facts.group: Things that raise BP: NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, steroids, oral contraceptives, heavy alcohol
decision_facts.why: A common, fixable cause of 'resistant' BP

decision_facts.group: Clues to a secondary cause: low potassium, sleep apnea, kidney disease, young age
decision_facts.why: Guideline recommends screening resistant hypertension for primary aldosteronism and other causes - verify 2025 scope

decision_facts.group: Signs of damage from BP: kidney function, urine albumin, prior stroke or heart disease
decision_facts.why: Raises urgency and the strength of treatment

decision_facts.group: LDL trend, statin dose, and any statin intolerance
decision_facts.why: LDL 190+ suggests inherited high cholesterol; on-statin LDL above goal may need added therapy

decision_facts.group: Existing heart disease, stroke or diabetes
decision_facts.why: Sets how low LDL and BP should go

not_seen: Often answerable by eConsult (medicine adjustment advice) without a visit
Suspected primary aldosteronism or other hormone cause (endocrinology)
review_notes: 2025 update: confirm 'severe hypertension' replaced 'hypertensive urgency' and that it is handled outpatient
2025 update: who should be screened for primary aldosteronism (all resistant HTN? broader?)
Whether bp_severe_no_symptoms belongs in 'urgent' (2 weeks) or is too high
Cholesterol source is not in the original list

review_questions: Are these the right red flags, and is anything emergent missing?
Should a stress test / coronary CT be pre-checked for chest pain, or always left to cardiology?
Is new AFib with a fast rate urgent, or emergent above some rate?
Do NICE's 2-week / 6-week heart failure rules map well onto urgent / routine in a US clinic?
BP: should the chart's own BP readings (last 14 days) count, or only what the PCP wrote?
For abnormal ECG, how should Lantern treat a bundle branch block when no prior ECG shows it is new?
Which reasons are most often fully answerable by eConsult?
